rv.q: Spitting Image in the rubbery flesh proved to be shockingly funny.
Ultimately, it’s the author’s treatment of Suella Braverman that is perhaps the most shocking.
More often, like those penises, the satire flops.
Right now, it feels like a lovingly crafted, highly skilled distraction from the political issues it should be making us care about.
It is huge fun, totally irreverent and takes no prisoners in the lampooning of our leaders and celebrity heroes.
This is a wonderfully funny show that doesn’t take itself seriously or shut anyone out.
Many jokes hit the spot, but not all.
While offering a visually dazzling feast, it only makes it more of a shame that the satire is the weakest aspect.
This isn’t satire so much as an Aunt Sally show where selected villains get to stand up and have the writers’ rotten vegetables thrown at them.
It all makes for an evening that ends up being very hit-and-miss with some genuine laugh-out-loud moments but also some distinctly dubious ones as well.
If this parade of people really does represent the future, we will need the refuge allowed by art more than ever.
The puppetry is first-class, of course.
Using everything from rod puppets, to half-body, to full skins and even a giant lettuce, this is a masterpiece of design and execution.
At its best, the satire hits home.

cn.t: Spitting Image's stage adaptation delivers impressive puppetry and occasional laughs, but critics find the satire more crude than cutting, with mixed results translating the TV format to theatre and struggles keeping pace with real-world politics.
